items.followUp: Differentiate between a group and a period in the periodic table.

rubric.why: Identifies what a group is and gives a characteristic of its elements.
rubric.description: Defines a group as a vertical column and states a shared characteristic.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a group as a vertical column and mentioning either the same number of valence electrons or similar chemical properties.

rubric.why: Identifies what a period is and gives a characteristic of its elements.
rubric.description: Defines a period as a horizontal row and states that its elements have the same number of shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a period as a horizontal row and stating that its elements have the same number of electron shells or energy levels.

modelAnswer: A group is a vertical column in the periodic table; its elements have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties.
A period is a horizontal row; its elements have the same number of electron shells.

items.followUp: Explain why atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group.

rubric.why: Connects the increase in nuclear pull across a period to the rise in ionization energy.
rubric.description: Explains the increase in ionization energy from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that nuclear charge or effective nuclear charge increases, causing stronger attraction for the outer electron.

rubric.why: Connects the increased distance or shielding down a group to the fall in ionization energy.
rubric.description: Explains the decrease in ionization energy down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that added shells increase distance or shielding, weakening the nucleus's attraction for the outer electron.

modelAnswer: Across a period, effective nuclear charge increases while the outer electrons remain in the same shell, so attraction to the nucleus increases and more energy is needed to remove an electron.
Down a group, additional shells increase the distance and shielding of the outer electron, so the nuclear attraction decreases and less energy is needed to remove it.

items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds generally have high melting points?

rubric.why: Identifies the strong attraction holding ions together.
rubric.description: States that ionic solids contain oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying oppositely charged ions and their strong electrostatic attraction.

rubric.why: Explains how the ions are arranged in the solid compound.
rubric.description: States that the ions form a rigid crystal lattice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the ions are arranged in a crystal lattice or held in fixed positions.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds consist of positively and negatively charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
The ions are arranged in a rigid crystal lattice, so ionic compounds are solid at room temperature.

items.followUp: Define melting point and give an example with a temperature.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of boiling point.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point as the temperature at which a liquid boils and changes into gas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition, including that the liquid changes into gas at that temperature.

rubric.why: Assesses whether the student gives a valid example and condition.
rubric.description: Gives water boiling at 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the example of water boiling at 100 °C at 1 atm (or standard atmospheric pressure).

modelAnswer: Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into gas throughout the liquid.
For example, water boils at 100 °C at 1 atm pressure.

items.followUp: State two factors that can cause an element to show allotropy.

rubric.why: Identifies a difference in the number of atoms in molecules as a cause of allotropy.
rubric.description: States that allotropes may differ in the number of atoms present in their molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning different numbers of atoms per molecule or a different molecular structure.

rubric.why: Identifies a difference in atomic arrangement as another cause of allotropy.
rubric.description: States that allotropes may differ in the arrangement of atoms in their structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning a different arrangement of atoms, such as in the crystal structure.

modelAnswer: Allotropy may be caused by different numbers of atoms in the molecules of an element.
It may also be caused by different arrangements of atoms in the structure of the element.

items.followUp: Define an alloy and give one example.

rubric.why: Assesses the defining nature of an alloy as a mixture.
rubric.description: Defines an alloy as a homogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an alloy as a homogeneous mixture.

rubric.why: Assesses the substances that may be combined to form an alloy.
rubric.description: States that an alloy contains two or more metals, or a metal mixed with a non-metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains two or more metals or a metal and a non-metal.

modelAnswer: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a non-metal.
For example, brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

items.followUp: Which solution is more concentrated: 0.5 M or 2 M? Explain briefly.

rubric.why: Assesses identification of the more concentrated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for choosing three molar (3 M).

rubric.why: Assesses understanding that molarity measures moles of solute per volume of solution.
rubric.description: Explains that the three-molar solution contains more solute per unit volume.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it has three moles of solute per dm³ (or litre), compared with one mole in the one-molar solution.

modelAnswer: The three-molar solution is more concentrated.
It contains 3 moles of solute per dm³ of solution, whereas a one-molar solution contains 1 mole per dm³.

items.followUp: What are electrolytes? Give one example.

rubric.why: Assesses the defining electrical behaviour of non-electrolytes.
rubric.description: States that non-electrolytes do not conduct electricity in solution or in the molten state because they do not form ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they do not conduct electricity and do not ionize or form ions.

rubric.why: Assesses whether a valid non-electrolyte example is given.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a non-electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as sugar, urea, or ethanol.

modelAnswer: Non-electrolytes are substances that do not form ions in solution or when molten and therefore do not conduct electricity.
Sugar is an example of a non-electrolyte.
